analysis.one_liner: Sets enforceable patient rights in managed care: emergency coverage, specialist access, outside appeals, and the right to sue.
analysis.headline: The Senate's Democratic leader introduced the bill with zero cosponsors; it was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar in June 1999, and no committee or floor vote ever followed before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Patients' Bill of Rights Act of 1999 would have set federal minimum protections for people in employer and private health plans: emergency care covered without prior approval at in-network rates, direct access to obstetricians and specialists, deadlines for plan decisions, binding outside appeals of denials, a ban on pay arrangements that reward denying care, and a federal right to sue a health plan for injuries caused by its decisions. The bill was never taken up by a committee and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in HMOs, group health plans, and private insurance. The bill targets the friction points of managed care: a patient who goes to the emergency room without approval, a woman who wants her OB/GYN as her regular doctor, a person with a chronic illness who needs standing referrals to a specialist, a family whose plan denies a treatment they appealed, and someone injured when a plan denies care. It also funds an independent ombudsman in each state to help people navigate grievances and appeals.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People in HMO and employer health plans

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans to cover emergency services without prior authorization, whether or not the provider is in-network, and caps what the patient can be billed at the in-network amount

Lets women designate an obstetrician-gynecologist directly as their primary care provider and get routine gynecological and pregnancy care without a referral, and requires standing referrals to specialists for ongoing conditions
Requires internal appeals with 72-hour deadlines in urgent cases, and a binding external appeals process conducted by an independent, conflict-free entity, with the plan paying the cost

Bars contracts that restrict what a doctor may tell a patient, prohibits pay arrangements that compensate utilization reviewers for the number of denials they issue, and sets deadlines (three business days for prior authorization, one business day for continued care) so decisions cannot be used as delay

Opens plans and insurers to state-law lawsuits for personal injury or wrongful death caused by their decisions about insurance, administrative, or medical services, while keeping most suits against employers out of court

Requires coverage of routine patient costs for people joining federally approved clinical trials, continuity of care for patients mid-treatment when a provider leaves the network, and inpatient stays after mastectomy for as long as the attending physician judges medically appropriate

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed care plans would bear the compliance costs, the cost of external appeals, and new lawsuit exposure; employers that sponsor plans would face new federal requirements, though the bill largely shields them from suits; premiums would likely reflect these costs over time. The bill's revenue title also reinstates Superfund excise taxes on crude oil and petroleum products and the corporate environmental tax, so those industries would pay the offsets. A companion provision requires a general-revenue transfer if the bill reduces Medicare trust-fund balances.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers, employers, petroleum and chemical makers

drawbacks.text: New coverage mandates and independent review requirements add administrative cost to every plan, and the bill allows plans to charge higher premiums or cost-sharing for the out-of-network point-of-service option it creates

The right to sue is narrower than some versions debated at the time: lawsuits for injury reach plans and insurers but generally not employers or plan sponsors, except when the sponsor personally exercises discretionary authority over a benefits claim and that causes injury, and some provisions bar class actions and limit relief to denied benefits plus attorney's fees

Insurers and employer groups argued during this era that a federal right to sue health plans would raise premiums and push some employers to drop coverage; how large that effect would be was the central contested question of the 1999-2001 patients' bill of rights debate

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the concrete protections are straightforward and address documented managed-care failures: surprise emergency bills, referral bottlenecks, slow and opaque denials, and no meaningful remedy. The genuine cost is administrative: internal and external review, network adequacy, quality data, and litigation exposure all cost money that flows into premiums, and the right to sue is the provision that most raised prices for employers and insurers. A reasonable design question is whether some of the same protections could be delivered with less litigation, which was the basis of the narrower competing bills of the era.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and read twice in June 1999 and placed on the Senate calendar, and then nothing happened: no committee took it up and no vote was ever scheduled before the 106th Congress expired.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Daschle introduced the bill on June 21, 1999; it was read the second time on June 22 and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 164
After being placed on the calendar, the bill received no further action, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 without a committee markup or any vote on it

The bill would have imposed the patient protections across three legal regimes covering employer and private coverage: the Public Health Service Act, ERISA, and the Internal Revenue Code, so that no type of group plan could escape the requirements
Its revenue title pays for the provisions in part by reinstating the Superfund excise taxes on crude oil and petroleum products through 2009 and the environmental tax through 2010

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed care plans were better off: they faced none of the bill's coverage mandates, appeal deadlines, network adequacy rules, or lawsuit exposure, and patients in managed care went without these protections for that Congress. A version of the issue resurfaced and stalled again in the next two Congresses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and managed care plans

for.name: Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders

against.name: Health insurance and managed care industry
against.role: Insurers and plans subject to the bill's mandates and lawsuit provision
against.what_they_did: Ran an extensive advertising and lobbying campaign in 1999-2000 against federal patients' bill of rights mandates and the right to sue health plans; this bill never reached a vote on which their position was recorded

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors, so partisan positions never showed on this measure; the era's broader patients'-bill-of-rights debate split largely along party lines, with Republicans favoring narrower versions without the right to sue.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: The bill requires emergency coverage without prior authorization, timely decisions, binding outside appeals, adequate networks, and bans paying reviewers based on the number of denials, and opens plans to state-law suits for injuries from their decisions. The bill failed, so none of these took effect; the industry's interest in this bill ran directly against the patients it would have protected.

Employers would face new compliance requirements and premiums would absorb some costs, but the bill largely shields them from lawsuits, allowing injury suits against a sponsor only when it personally exercised discretionary authority over a claim. Their interest was avoiding the mandates; the bill partially accommodated them.

Plans could not deny coverage of a drug or device use that appears in its FDA-authorized labeling on the ground that it is investigational, and must allow formulary exceptions when a non-formulary alternative is medically indicated. That means more covered sales, and patients get the drugs, so the industry's interest and patients' interest run together here.
The bill's revenue title reinstates Superfund excise taxes on crude oil and petroleum products and the environmental tax as offsets, so these industries would pay for the bill's cost provisions.
